#9663. Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

The team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

#9662. 20 Repos, 713K Stars: The Open Source Tools That Build, Tune and Run Language Models

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

huggingface/transformers is the most-starred repo in the whole directory, at 169.4K. This week it added 100 stars. OpenVINO, Intel's inference toolkit, has 12.8K stars and added 1.3K, thirteen times as many. That gap says where the work is now. Most teams no longer write a model from scratch. They pick one that already exists, tune it on their own data, and then fight to make it run fast and cheap on the hardware they have.

Every repo below comes from TextMining.Tech, HackerNoon's directory of 7,075 open source text mining tools, libraries and frameworks with at least 100 stars each. They're grouped by job: define the model, train or fine-tune it, then run it.

This is part 2 of a four-part series. Part 1 covered the tools that read documents, retrieve context and teach you to build. Speech and voice come next.

These repos hold the models themselves, or the code and data that define them. transformers is the hub most of the others plug into; the rest are model families built for a language, a domain or a different way of answering.

The model-definition framework for text, vision, audio and multimodal models, for inference and training

Non-autoregressive engine that makes typed choice, score and yes/no decisions over text in one forward pass, in 100+ languages

Microsoft's large-scale self-supervised pre-training across tasks, languages and modalities

Ready-to-use datasets for AI models, with tools to load and transform them

Alibaba Cloud's official repo for the original Qwen chat and pretrained models

Open source financial LLMs, with trained models released on Hugging Face

Chinese LLaMA and Alpaca models, with local CPU and GPU training and deployment

laya added nearly three times as many stars as transformers this week, from a base a fifth the size.

Once you have a base model, these repos adapt it to your data or train new ones at scale. They range from a one-stop fine-tuning toolkit to the distributed systems behind frontier-scale training, plus two 2023-era projects that taught a generation how instruction tuning works.

Unified, efficient fine-tuning for 100+ LLMs and vision-language models (ACL 2024)

Distributed compute engine with libraries for scaling training and other ML workloads

Community-built chat assistant project, including its crowd-sourced training data

Code and data generation for training Stanford's Alpaca instruction-tuned models

An open book on the engineering of training and running large models

NVIDIA's research code for training transformer models at scale

White Circle's framework for training large language and multimodal models

halo is the smallest repo in this series so far, and it added more stars this week than anything else in this group.

A tuned model is only useful once it answers requests. These repos run models locally, compile them for phones and browsers, wire them into apps, and watch what they do in production.

Self-hosted engine that runs LLMs, vision, voice, image and video models on any hardware, no GPU required

AI engineering platform with a gateway, agent observability, evals and prompt management, built on OpenTelemetry

Vercel's AI SDK for building AI-powered apps and agents in TypeScript

Universal LLM deployment engine that uses ML compilation to target many devices

High-performance LLM inference that runs inside the browser

Toolkit for optimizing and deploying AI inference

The smallest repo in this group gained the most: OpenVINO's 1.3K stars this week topped the whole Natural Language Processing category.

All numbers come from the TextMining.Tech snapshot of Nov 26, 2026. The directory tracks open source GitHub repos with at least 100 stars, excludes archived repos and forks, and refreshes daily. We started from the top repos in the Language Models and Natural Language Processing categories and kept the ones that define, train or run models. "Added this week" is the directory's own weekly star count. Stars will have moved by the time you read this, so each repo name links to its live directory page.

Part 3 is speech and voice. VoiceStudio, a fully local voice cloning, dubbing and transcription suite, added 4.9K stars this week, more than all 20 repos in this list combined.

#9661. Website or mobile app: which should your organization build first?

Posted on Nov 28 • Originally published at blog.ahmed-adil.com

"We want an app" is one of the most common first sentences in a project meeting. Sometimes it is exactly right. Often, a well-built mobile website would reach more people, sooner, for less.

1. How often will people use it? An app earns its place on a phone when people open it every week or every day: checking tickets, tracking orders, scanning at a gate. If people visit a few times a year, they will not install anything. A website meets them where they already are: in a search result or a shared link.

2. Does it need the phone itself? Camera scanning, offline mode, background location or push notifications are where apps shine. If none of these matter, the browser can do almost everything.

3. How do people find you? Search engines index websites, not apps. If new visitors come from Google, a website is your front door, and an app can be the next step for loyal users.

4. Who will maintain it? An app means two stores, review processes and updates for new phone versions. That is fine with a plan and a budget; it is painful without one.

For most societies, companies and service providers, the right order is:

Whatever you start with, build the backend so it can serve a website, a dashboard and an app later. Then adding the app is a new front door, not a second project.

Largely, yes. A modern website can be installed on the home screen, work fast on mobile and even send some notifications. It cannot fully replace camera-heavy or offline-first tools.

Usually not. A cross-platform framework such as Flutter builds both from one codebase, which keeps cost and maintenance down.

Not sure which one you need? Tell the editor about your users on ahmed-adil.com and Ahmed will help you decide.

#9660. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

#9659. Typed API Contracts from NestJS to Next.js with OpenAPI: openapi-typescript, openapi-fetch, and Where the Types Lie — Field Notes

Posted on Nov 28 • Originally published at devya.dev

Headline: The most reliable way I have found to keep a Next.js frontend in sync with a NestJS REST API is to treat the OpenAPI spec as the contract: the @nestjs/swagger CLI plugin generates the spec at build time, openapi-typescript turns it into TypeScript types, and openapi-fetch makes every call type-checked. A CI step that regenerates both files and runs git diff --exit-code turns an unannounced contract change into a failed build instead of a production bug.

For a long time my Next.js apps talked to NestJS backends through types I copied by hand, or at best through a shared types package in the monorepo. Both drifted. A renamed field compiled fine on the frontend and rendered undefined in production. These are my notes from replacing that with generated types, including the places where generated types still lie.

Shared TypeScript types drift because they describe what the backend code intends, not what goes over the wire. A NestJS DTO with createdAt: Date arrives in the browser as an ISO 8601 string, because JSON has no date type. A global interceptor that wraps every response in { data } changes the shape without touching the DTO. And a shared types package only helps TypeScript clients in the same repository; a React Native app in another repo gets nothing.

An OpenAPI spec is a JSON or YAML document that lists every path, parameter, request body, and response schema of an HTTP API. Generating frontend types from the spec moves the source of truth one step closer to the wire, and it gives non-TypeScript clients the same contract.

An accurate NestJS spec starts with the @nestjs/swagger CLI plugin, a TypeScript compiler transformer that adds @ApiProperty() metadata to every property in files ending in .dto.ts or .entity.ts, and response metadata based on each controller method's return type. Without the plugin, every DTO property needs a hand-written @ApiProperty(), and the ones you forget do not exist in the spec.

I export the spec from a small script that compiles with the rest of the app, instead of downloading it from a running server:

Three details mattered. First, the Swagger plugin is a TypeScript transformer, so it runs in nest build but not under tsx or esbuild, which strip types without running transformers; my first spec came out of tsx with empty DTO schemas. Second, NestFactory.create() instantiates providers, so an async provider that opens a database connection will try to connect; in CI I point the export step at the same throwaway Postgres the tests use. Third, I commit openapi.json, so a reviewer sees every contract change as a diff next to the code that caused it.

openapi-typescript converts an OpenAPI 3.x document into one .d.ts file that exports a paths type, and openapi-fetch uses that type to check the URL, path parameters, query, body, and response of every call. Neither tool emits runtime code per endpoint, which is why I prefer them over generators that produce a client class per controller.

In the Next.js App Router I create the client per request. A module-level client with an auth middleware is shared by every request the server handles, and that is exactly how one user's token ends up on another user's call.

A typo in '/orders/{id}', a missing path parameter, or a field the DTO no longer has is now a compile error. Once the controller declares its error responses, data and error narrow like a discriminated union. After I regenerate the types, renaming a field in a NestJS DTO breaks next build wherever the frontend reads it, which is the whole point.

Generated types are only as honest as the spec, and the NestJS spec is built from decorators and class metadata, not from the bytes the API actually returns. These are the gaps I hit:

None of this validates responses at runtime: openapi-fetch trusts the server. My NestJS e2e tests validate a handful of critical responses against the committed openapi.json, which is what caught the interceptor wrapper for me.

A contract drift check regenerates the OpenAPI spec and the frontend types on every pull request and fails if either differs from what is committed. In a pnpm monorepo it is four steps:

The diff check catches forgotten regeneration; it does not judge whether a change is safe. When an API has clients that do not deploy together with it, such as a mobile app already in the stores, I also run oasdiff breaking with --fail-on ERR against the spec from the main branch. oasdiff is an OpenAPI diff tool, and it fails the build when a change removes a response field or makes an optional request field required.

OpenAPI codegen is the right choice when the NestJS API already exists as REST controllers or serves clients that are not written in TypeScript. tRPC and ts-rest are better when you control both ends and want the contract written in TypeScript first.

My backends already had REST controllers and Swagger UI, and some of them also serve a React Native app, so generating from OpenAPI meant no rewrite and one contract for every client.

Q: Does openapi-fetch add much to my Next.js bundle?

A: Very little. openapi-fetch is a small wrapper around the native fetch, and the openapi-typescript output is a .d.ts file that compiles away completely.

Q: Should I commit the generated openapi.json and schema.d.ts?

A: Yes. Committing both files makes API contract changes visible in code review and gives the CI drift check something to compare against.

Q: Why do NestJS Date fields come out as string in the generated types?

A: JSON has no date type, so NestJS serializes a Date as an ISO 8601 string and the spec marks it type: string, format: date-time. openapi-typescript keeps it a string, which is correct; parse it where you need a date.

Q: Can a React Native app use the same generated client?

A: Yes. openapi-fetch only depends on the global fetch, which React Native provides, so a mobile app can import the same paths type from a shared package or a copy of schema.d.ts.

Q: Do I need Swagger UI enabled in production for this to work?

A: No. The spec is written by a build-time script, and the typed client only needs the committed openapi.json. Exposing Swagger UI with SwaggerModule.setup() is a separate, optional decision.

#9656. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

In 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

You must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

Yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9654. Edge Code Sandbox via Valkey Streams and Docker BuildKit

Posted on Nov 28 • Originally published at bijaktechnology.com

💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

When a thousand students or software developers click "Run Code" simultaneously on an EduTech platform or interactive coding environment, edge node infrastructures face massive disk I/O thrashing and severe CPU core spikes. Without precise queue orchestration and a resilient container layer caching strategy, the system quickly succumbs to cache stampedes, exponentially multiplying compilation latencies until hitting kernel-level Out-Of-Memory (OOM) panics. Building a secure, responsive, and resource-efficient code sandbox at edge nodes requires a fundamental paradigm shift: pairing the high-throughput asynchronous event streams of Valkey with Docker BuildKit's multi-stage build caching architecture.

In real-world production setups, pushing execution requests to edge workers must never block the main API gateway. By combining Valkey Streams as a high-performance lock-free queue buffer and Docker BuildKit configured with local inline caching, the execution node can isolate user code compilation without repeatedly downloading base runtime dependencies (such as C++ standard headers, Python packages, or node_modules) over external network interfaces.

This deep-dive technical guide explores the architectural integration of Valkey Streams and Docker BuildKit to safely process isolated code execution on distributed nodes hosted on Hostinger KVM VPS infrastructure, ensuring strict system stability and high operational throughput.

LaFinteca connects global merchants directly to local payment rails across Latin America, cutting out the intermediaries that sit between a checkout and the actual transaction.

The starting point is a straightforward observation: each country in the region runs on its own rules and infrastructure. Pix in Brazil, SPEI in Mexico, PSE in Colombia, they don’t work the same way, and they don’t talk to each other. LaFinteca’s answer is a single API that covers more than 20 local payment methods across 30 markets, so a merchant adding a new country changes a configuration, not a codebase. A sandbox environment lets engineering teams test each market against real payment logic before going live.

The company holds a license from Brazil’s Banco Central do Brasil, the most heavily regulated payments market in the region, and operates under local regulatory frameworks in the other markets it covers. In Brazil, it is also a member of ABFintechs, the national fintech association, which gives it a formal channel with the BCB.

LaFinteca reports over 41 million transactions processed to date. The platform runs on direct connections, which means decline reasons and routing decisions reach the merchant rather than stopping at an intermediary.

#9651. Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

Three issues were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each new process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

On the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

On the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:

The person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

These videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

#9650. Fix Presigned URLs With an Internal Docker Hostname: Sign for the Address the Browser Can Reach

Posted on Nov 28 • Originally published at opndrive.app

Your app runs in Docker Compose next to an S3-compatible server such as MinIO, RustFS, Garage or SeaweedFS. It signs a presigned URL for the browser, and the URL starts with http://minio:9000, the Compose service name. The browser can’t use that address, and if you edit the host by hand, the server answers SignatureDoesNotMatch. An open October 2026 issue asks for exactly this: presigned URLs that “use a host the browser can reach (localhost, not the compose service name)” (candiedoperation/TechOps #108).

Below are the cause, a curl check that tells the failures apart, and the fix in the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 and boto3, then the path-style and region settings that break it next. Once the host is right, the browser still needs a CORS rule on that endpoint.

Nothing below has been run for this post; it is built from the documentation linked at each step, so try it on a throwaway stack first.

A presigned URL is valid only for the host it was signed for, because Signature Version 4 signs the Host header. Your SDK builds the URL locally from the endpoint you gave it, so a client set to http://minio:9000 signs for minio:9000. Sign with a second client whose endpoint is the address the browser uses.

AWS’s signing rules say you must include “the host header (HTTP/1.1) or the :authority header (HTTP/2)” in the signature (AWS, Create a signed AWS API request). The Host header holds the host and the port (RFC 9110, section 7.2), so minio:9000, localhost:9000 and files.example.com (example) are three different signed values for one server.

The server checks the Host it actually received. MinIO’s verifier reads a signed host header from the incoming request (extractedSignedHeaders.Set(header, r.Host) in signature-v4-utils.go) and returns ErrSignatureDoesNotMatch when its recomputed signature differs (signature-v4.go). SeaweedFS’s wiki states the same rule (SeaweedFS, S3 Nginx Proxy), and RustFS’s docs say the hostname, scheme, port, region and object path “must match the values used to sign the URL” (RustFS, S3 protocol).

In Compose, containers reach each other by service name, service-to-service traffic uses the container port, and “the host port is only used when accessing the service from outside the network” (Docker, Networking in Compose). The browser sits outside that network, so it reaches only the published port, such as localhost:9000, or a public domain in front of it.

Presigning makes no network call, which is why the fix works. AWS says “Creating a presigned URL happens locally” (AWS, presigned URLs), and Cloudflare says R2 presigned URLs are generated “with no communication with R2” (Cloudflare R2, Presigned URLs). So the app container can sign for the browser’s address without connecting to it.

Sign the URL for the address the browser can reach: localhost:9000 works from outside Compose, rustfs:9000 does not. Drawn from Docker’s Compose networking docs, not from a live run.

Start with the URL itself: its host and port are the signed host, and the X-Amz-SignedHeaders query parameter lists the signed headers (Cloudflare R2, Presigned URLs). To confirm, run curl from your machine, not from a container. is the URL your app printed, and the single quotes keep its & characters intact:

These outcomes are predicted from the signing rules; no test run has captured them yet:

Editing minio:9000 to localhost:9000 in a signed URL changes the Host the server receives, so its recomputed signature no longer matches.

You may see MINIO_SERVER_URL suggested as the fix. MinIO’s docs mark it “Deprecated since version RELEASE.2024-05-10T01-41-38Z” and describe it in terms of Console logins, with nothing about presigned URLs (MinIO AIStor, deprecated settings). Your SDK computes the URL inside your app, so no server environment variable can change a URL your app has already signed. Where a setup with it works, check whether the app’s client already points at the public domain.

Keep two clients with the same keys, region and path-style setting. The internal client uses http://rustfs:9000 for every server-side call. The presign client uses the browser’s address and only signs: http://localhost:9000 in development, or a public domain such as https://files.example.com (example) in production.

This example runs RustFS, which uses the image rustfs/rustfs, serves the S3 API on port 9000 and the Console on 9001, and reads its root keys from RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY and RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY (RustFS, Docker install). Values in angle brackets are placeholders. Set your own root keys before the stack is reachable from a network: RustFS’s docs say port 9000 also carries administrative and internode traffic, so do not expose it without network and IAM controls (RustFS, S3 protocol).

If you publish 9100:9000 instead, the public endpoint becomes http://localhost:9100 and the internal one stays http://rustfs:9000, because containers talk on the container port (Docker, Networking in Compose). For other options, see RustFS’s Docker guide.

On Garage, use the port and region from its quick start: S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT=http://garage:3900, S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:3900 and S3_REGION=garage, with garage as the example service name (Garage, quick start).

On MinIO, the fix is the same, with http://minio:9000 as the internal endpoint. The minio/minio repository was archived on April 25, 2026, and its README says the community edition “is now distributed as source code only”, so a Compose file that pulls a ready-made image may fail. We did not check the image registries; use the MinIO image you already run.

The signer needs a bucket, an object and a key. These RustFS steps follow its docs for creating a bucket, uploading an object and access keys:

On Garage, the quick start’s environment variables create the bucket and key. Put the new key into S3_ACCESS_KEY and S3_SECRET_KEY, and scope that key to one bucket.

The module checks the object through the internal client, then signs a GET URL with the presign client. getSignedUrl from @aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner takes the client, the command and expiresIn in seconds, which defaults to 900 (@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner README). Untested: it has not run against a demo server.

The option name forcePathStyle comes from LocalStack’s SDK guide (LocalStack, AWS SDK for JavaScript); the official reference did not load for us, so check it against the S3ClientConfig type in your installed @aws-sdk/client-s3. For uploads, sign a PutObjectCommand with the same presign client; if you set ContentType, the browser must send a matching Content-Type header (Cloudflare R2, aws-sdk-js-v3).

The script sets signature_version="s3v4" because the Host rule above is the Signature Version 4 rule, and AWS’s boto3 guide recommends s3v4 for presigned URLs (Boto3, presigned URLs). generate_presigned_url expires after 3600 seconds by default (Boto3, generate_presigned_url), so the script sets 900. Untested, like the JavaScript module.

Keep the expiry short in both: AWS calls presigned URLs “bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them” (AWS, presigned URLs).

Virtual-hosted style puts the bucket name into the hostname (AWS, virtual hosting), giving hosts such as .localhost:9000 or .rustfs:9000; Garage’s docs say this style needs a wildcard DNS entry (Garage, configuration). LocalStack’s guide says the JavaScript v3 client uses virtual-host addressing by default, and boto3’s default, auto, “Attempts to use virtual, but falls back to path if necessary” (Boto3, configuration). So both programs set path-style explicitly. AWS’s boto3 guide recommends virtual-hosted style for presigning, advice meant for Amazon S3 itself.

The region sits in the signature’s credential scope, which “restricts the resulting signature to the specified Region and service” (AWS, Create a signed AWS API request). A wrong region can fail even when the host is right, and no single value fits every server:

In production, sign with the public HTTPS URL the browser uses, which RustFS calls “the externally reachable endpoint” (RustFS, S3 protocol). The proxy must pass on the Host the browser sent, since MinIO verifies against the Host it receives. Garage needs a proxy for HTTPS anyway: its S3 endpoint “does not support TLS” (Garage, configuration). SeaweedFS can pin the host it verifies with -s3.externalUrl, or rebuild it from X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Port (SeaweedFS, S3 Nginx Proxy). We have no tested proxy config to show.

Run the signer in the app container, whose image must contain the script and its packages, then request the printed URL from your machine:

If the fix works, curl gets HTTP 200 and the URL opens in the browser. If curl works but a browser upload from your page is blocked, look at CORS: on MinIO, set MinIO’s server-wide origin list (MINIO_API_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN); AIStor also accepts per-bucket rules that override it. On other servers, add a CORS rule on the bucket that allows your page’s origin.

Any browser client follows the same rule: if you run a self-hosted Opndrive next to a local server, enter the endpoint the browser can reach, such as http://localhost:9000, because the guide to connecting storage says the browser talks to S3 directly.

Opndrive gives any S3-compatible bucket a Drive-like web interface you host yourself. See it on GitHub or read the docs.

#9649. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.
